chunks: Ali ibn al-Hakam from Rahim said:

I said to Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him): 'I am your ransom; I see that when you pray and raise your head from prostration in the first and third rak'ah, you sit upright, then stand up. So we do as you do.' He said, 'Do not look at what I do.' Indeed, he (peace be upon him) said, 'Do not look at what I do,' lest they believe that this is obligatory upon them. It did not prevent him from being imitated in his action as a supererogatory act and seeking perfection. Sitting between the two prostrations and between prostration and standing is from the etiquettes of prayer, not its obligatory duties. And that which clarifies what we mentioned is what he narrated:

key_terms.الرِّضَا: Al-Rida (the Accepting One), a title of the 8th Imam

ai.seo_question: Why did Imam al-Rida advise against strictly imitating his prayer posture?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) clarified that his specific sitting posture after the first and third rak'ah was a supererogatory etiquette (adab) for spiritual perfection rather than an obligatory duty (fard), preventing followers from mistakenly elevating his personal practice to a mandatory requirement. This distinction highlights the Shia scholarly principle of differentiating between the essential pillars of prayer and the recommended nuances that reflect the Imam's unique status, ensuring that legal obligations remain clear while encouraging emulation for spiritual excellence.
